## 5. Analysis plan summary (for public registration before access)

This is not a form field. It outlines the plan EVA will register publicly before it accesses any UK Biobank data
[TO CONFIRM: which public registry]. The pass marks come from version 3's charter (`ml/biological-age/CHARTER.md`) and
cannot change after registration. Details marked "to fix" are settled in the registered plan, before access.

### 5.1 Version 3 in brief (from EVA's files)

- **Method.** The PhenoAge method of Levine et al. 2018, re-estimated: a Gompertz proportional-hazards model of
  all-cause mortality with an elastic-net penalty, converted to years. The years are age plus an acceleration measured
  against people of the same sex and age (`MODEL-CARD.md`, sections 8, 9 and 11).
- **Data.** US NHANES: training 1988 to 1994; validation 1999 to 2006; sealed test 2007 to 2014; an independent check on
  2015 to 2018 data without mortality (`CHARTER.md`, section 3).
- **Sealed test, Base tier** (9,978 people, 608 deaths): hazard ratio 1.516 per SD of acceleration (95% CI 1.412 to
  1.629); gain in C-statistic over age and sex 0.0217 (0.0131 to 0.0299); every sex and age band within 0.74 years
  (`REPORT.md`).
- **Comparator on the same people.** The original PhenoAge, which needs a blood count and glucose: hazard ratio 1.583,
  C gain 0.0313 (`REPORT.md`).
- **Disclosures for the paper** (`REPORT.md`, `MODEL-CARD.md`):
  - the sealed test was run twice, the second time after a fix prompted by the first;
  - the plan was amended after the 2015 to 2018 check;
  - the charter was time-stamped in EVA's code repository, not in a public registry;
  - the Base result moved by 2.6 years between two NHANES cycles, most likely because of a change of laboratory methods;
  - hs-CRP below 2.1 mg/L counts as 2.1, because the 1988 to 1994 survey measured nothing lower;
  - the NHANES results are unweighted, except a survey-weighted re-analysis of the 2003 to 2006 validation data. In it
    the mortality association held (hazard ratio 1.44 per SD, against 1.38 unweighted) and the model read about 0.4
    years younger than age (`sensitivity/WEIGHTED.md`).
- **Status.** Not published, not validated outside NHANES, and not shown to clients.

### 5.2 What is tested

- The frozen file `ml/biological-age/model-v3.json`: file SHA-256
  `367072a01cf8edf730f117c0ec4145dd3b5c0f18b980c43aa901bdd95539caa6`, model_sha256
  `dc60ee29d88621c716086434c9894779417a3189fe7c2ee5178f010eec45bb10` (`MODEL-CARD.md`).
- Two tiers: Base (albumin, ALP, hs-CRP, creatinine, BUN, GGT) and Base + HbA1c.
- Applied once. No refitting, no recalibration, no change to clamps or caps.
- The blood-count tier is not part of version 3 and is not tested.

### 5.3 Who is included

- Participants with all markers of the tier at the baseline visit (instance 0). Complete cases only, with no imputation,
  as in version 3.
- Ages 37 to 73 at recruitment (field 21022), inside version 3's range of 20 to 84.
- Excluded: pregnancy (field 3140 = Yes; the rule for "Unsure" to fix).
- Withdrawn participants are removed as UK Biobank instructs.

### 5.4 Inputs and units

- Albumin and C-reactive protein are divided by 10 (g/L to g/dL; mg/L to mg/dL), as `MODEL-CARD.md` section 9 states.
- Creatinine (umol/L), urea (mmol/L, converted to BUN) and HbA1c (mmol/mol, converted to % by the IFCC to NGSP master
  equation EVA already uses, `PROPOSAL.md` condition 3) use conversion constants written into the plan.
- The frozen clamps and the CRP rule apply: CRP below 2.1 mg/L counts as 2.1, and CRP above 10 mg/L is capped at 10 and
  flagged.
- Results UK Biobank marks as not reportable: rule to fix, using the reportability fields.

### 5.5 Outcome and follow-up

- **Primary outcome:** death from any cause, from the death register (fields 40000 and 40023). The rule for people with
  more than one death record is to fix.
- **Follow-up** runs from the baseline visit date (field 53, instance 0) to the earliest of death, loss to follow-up
  (field 191), or the censoring date for the participant's country. UK Biobank's suggested dates are 31 August 2024 for
  England and Wales and 30 November 2024 for Scotland. UK Biobank calls these "guidance only", so they are re-checked at
  access and fixed in the plan. Country comes from the assessment centre (field 54).
- **Secondary:** deaths by broad underlying cause (field 40001), reported only.

### 5.6 Pass marks, fixed now

These are the charter's tests T2, T3, T4 and T8 with the charter's thresholds. Version 3 counts as validated in UK
Biobank only if every one of them passes. Confidence intervals use 1,000 bootstrap resamples, as in the charter.

| Test | Pass mark |
|---|---|
| Ranking of risk (T2) | Hazard ratio per SD of acceleration, from a Cox model with age and sex: lower 95% bound at least 1.20. Gain in cross-fitted Harrell's C over age and sex: above 0, with a 95% interval that excludes 0. |
| Level (T3) | Mean biological age minus age within 1.0 year overall and within 1.5 years in each sex and age band. Slope of biological age on age 0.85 to 1.15. Gompertz calibration slope for 10-year mortality 0.8 to 1.2. |
| Base + HbA1c (T2 and T4) | C-statistic at least Base minus 0.001 on the same people. Mean of Base minus Base + HbA1c within 0.5 years overall and 1.0 year in each band. |
| Subgroups (T8) | Hazard ratio lower bound above 1.0 in men, in women, under 60 and at 60 and over. Point estimate above 1.0 in each ethnic group with at least 50 deaths. |

The charter's bands are 20 to 39, 40 to 59 and 60 to 84. Ages at recruitment in UK Biobank start at 37 (field 21022),
so the youngest band would hold only people aged 37 to 39. The rule for them is to fix. The charter's comparison with
EVA's previous model (KDM v2.2) is not part of this plan.

### 5.7 Comparators, subgroups and sensitivity analyses (reported, not pass marks)

- **Comparators on the same people:** age and sex alone; the original PhenoAge with its published coefficients.
- **Subgroups:** sex; age band; ethnic background (field 21000); fifths of the Townsend deprivation index (field 189);
  country.
- **Sensitivity analyses:** leaving out the first 2 years of follow-up; leaving out CRP above 10 mg/L instead of capping
  it; by fasting time (field 74).

### 5.8 Aim 2: add-on modules

- **Method:** as EVA's add-on program (`ml/biological-age/addons/REPORT.md`, section 2). An add-on adds a term for the
  part of a marker's value that age, sex and the six Base markers do not predict. Its weight comes from a Gompertz model
  of mortality with version 3 as a fixed offset.
- **Splits:** before any outcome is examined, eligible participants are split at random into training, validation and a
  sealed test part. Proportions to fix. A hash of each ID list is recorded. The sealed part is read once.
- **Candidates:** cystatin C first. EVA could not test it in NHANES for lack of data. Then the Base Panel tests not in
  version 3: apolipoprotein B, ALT, urate, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides.
- **Rules:** as the add-on charter. Right direction (`CHARTER.md`, section 5), survival of the penalty, a better
  validation C-statistic, and the noise and composition tests.
- **Vitamin D is described only.** EVA's add-on report sets a condition: "evidence that raising it lowers mortality,
  before any term credits a higher value" (`addons/REPORT.md`, section 8). So no vitamin D term enters the client age
  from this work.

### 5.9 Aim 3: change between the two visits

- People with all Base markers at the baseline visit and the repeat visit (instance 1).
- Describe the change in biological age minus age, and the share whose change is larger than version 3's 95% reliable
  change, about 4.3 years for Base (`REPORT.md`). Descriptive only.

### 5.10 Aim 4: sample handling and laboratory

- Does the acceleration vary with assay date (for example field 30601), the estimated sample dilution factor (30897),
  fasting time (74) or the time of the blood draw (3166)?
- **Level against the US data, marker by marker.** UK Biobank ran each test with one method, for example albumin by
  bromocresol green and creatinine by an enzymatic method. Albumin's method and enzymatic creatinine are the methods
  that matter most for version 3 (`PROPOSAL.md`, condition 1). UK Biobank data alone cannot separate laboratory
  differences from population differences. The report will say so.
- **Why this matters.** The samples were taken in 2006 to 2010 but assayed later: albumin, for example, between
  1 November 2015 and 3 October 2017 (field 30601).

### 5.11 Reporting

- The TRIPOD reporting checklist for prediction models, as used for version 3's model card.
- Every cell in a published table has at least 10 participants.
- "UK Biobank" in the title or abstract, and the acknowledgement: "This research has been conducted using the UK Biobank
  Resource under application number [ ]."

EVA publishes the failure. EVA does not describe version 3 as validated, and reviews the model under a new

## 6. How EVA will handle the data

These follow UK Biobank's rules and the MTA. The copy read is the data-only MTA for new applicants, 2023, version 1.4,
dated 26 October 2023.

- **Analysis only on the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP).** Individual-level data never leave it. No
  download exemption is requested.
- **Training.** Everyone with access completes UK Biobank's four modules first: the MRC course, "Introduction to using UK
  Biobank", "Introduction to the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP)" and "Code repository training".
- **No identification.** No attempt to identify, link or contact any participant. Any accidental identification is
  reported to UK Biobank at once.
- **No sharing.** The data are not shared, sold or sub-licensed.
- **Security incidents** are reported within 24 hours.
- **Small numbers.** At least 10 participants in every published table cell.
- **Reports.** An annual report every year. Every report and press release goes to UK Biobank at least 2 weeks before
  release, and press releases that mention UK Biobank go to its press team first.
- **Publication.** All reasonable efforts to publish within 6 months of the project end date.
- **End of project.** The data are destroyed, and EVA confirms this in writing to access@ukbiobank.ac.uk.

"}, {"name": "STEPS.md", "content": "# UK Biobank: the CEO's steps to register and apply

Prepared on 29 October 2026 for Juan Diego Lago. It goes with `APPLICATION.md`, which holds the form text. Every UK
Biobank fact was read on 29 October 2026 from the sources listed at the end. Nothing has been done yet: no account, no
email sent, no money committed.

## Where things stand today

- **New applications are closed.** The AMS login page: "We are currently not accepting new applications to UK
  Biobank, as the UKB-RAP remains closed." UK Biobank aims to reopen them "in late 2026". No date is confirmed.
- **Registrations are paused.** Since 18 August 2026, registrations, extensions and change requests are not processed.
  Requests sent during the pause "will be automatically closed". UK Biobank recommends waiting for its update. None
  was found on 29 October 2026.
- **Death records are not available yet.** UK Biobank is waiting for the UK health data controllers and the Government
  to agree before researchers can see health outcome data again. EVA's study needs the death register.
- **No results can leave the platform at first.** A manual output check will be piloted this year with a small number
  of users. An automated one is planned for 2027.
- **What EVA can do now:** prepare everything, and ask UK Biobank a feasibility question. UK Biobank's FAQ: "UK Biobank
  is happy to respond to general questions, such as whether a research project is feasible using the resource".
- **What not to do now:** sign up in AMS. UK Biobank asks people to sign up only when they wish to apply, and
  registrations sent during the pause are closed automatically.

## Stage 1. Now: decide and prepare

| # | Action | Who | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Decide who is the Applicant PI, whether to bring in an academic partner (option A or B), and who signs the MTA | CEO | `APPLICATION.md`, section 1. The PI must apply in their own name. The MTA signatory cannot be the PI. |
| 2 | Review and send the feasibility email to access@ukbiobank.ac.uk | CEO | Draft supplied separately. It asks about the data tier, EVA's eligibility as an institution, and access to death records and results. It does not say EVA has applied. UK Biobank's Access Procedures send queries about registration, applications and the MTA to this address. The Community's "Submit a request" form (https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/requests/new) is the other route. |
| 3 | If a partner is chosen, agree the terms with them | CEO, with counsel | Roles, authorship, intellectual property, and who pays the £1,000 fee for an extra institution. The Toledo Study team could serve both the UK Biobank and the Spanish validation (`DECISION.md`, section 5.3). |
| 4 | Make EVA's website pass the institution check | CEO | It must show EVA's activities, location and email domain, and be reachable from abroad. Add profile pages for the researchers if they will not send CVs. |
| 5 | Give each researcher and the MTA signatory a personal @evahealth.es address | CEO | Registration needs "An email account that is specific to you and your institute". The MTA contact cannot use a public email domain. |
| 6 | Collect each researcher's documents | Each researcher | Full name and date of birth; CV in English or a profile page on EVA's website; PubMed IDs of up to 5 papers, if any; any complaints in the last 3 years. |
| 7 | Take the MRC course "Confidentiality and Data Protection in Health Research" | Each researcher | Pass mark 70%. The certificate must be less than 12 months old, so take it shortly before registering. |
| 8 | Install the Microsoft Authenticator app | Each researcher | AMS now asks users to "confirm their identity through the Microsoft Authenticator app". |
| 9 | Ask counsel to read the MTA, and to check Spanish ethics, data protection and VAT | CEO, counsel | The MTA cannot be negotiated and is under the law of England and Wales. UK Biobank's pages say nothing about Spanish requirements. |
| 10 | Finish the analysis plan and register it publicly | Analysis lead [TO CONFIRM] | `APPLICATION.md`, section 5. Settle every "to fix" item. Registration must happen before any data access. |
| 11 | Approve the budget | CEO | See "Costs" below. |
| 12 | Decide on UK Biobank's Scientific Conference, 10 December 2026, London and online | CEO | Virtual tickets from 1 November. UK Biobank's team "will be on hand to offer in-person support with accessing the re-launched UKB-RAP and making new applications". Ticket price not found. |
| 13 | Let DocuSign emails through | EVA's email administrator | UK Biobank sends the MTA only by DocuSign, from the domain @eumail.docusign.net. |
| 14 | Watch the Researcher Community | CEO | https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb. Wait for three notices: applications reopen, registrations resume, health outcome data are back. |

## Stage 2. When applications reopen: sign up, apply, register

1. **Sign up** on the AMS home page, https://ams.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ams/. UK Biobank suggests "a long term,
   non-institutional email address as a contact email address" for sign-up, because affiliations change. Open the
   verification link within 24 hours.
2. **Choose the application type:** "Data only".
3. **Fill in the application form** from `APPLICATION.md`, section 3: A1, A2, A3, A4.1, A4.2, A5.1, A6 if shown, and
   B1. Check every character count in AMS. Proofread A1 and A2: UK Biobank publishes them exactly as submitted.
4. **Collaborators tab:** the institute where the work is done; collaborators at EVA; collaborators at other institutes.
   Only registered and approved researchers can be added, but new ones can be invited.
5. **MTA details:** EVA's full legal name and the MTA contact, who is not the PI.
6. **Registration form:** it follows the application form. It covers identity, documents and the institution. EVA as an
   institution must be "registered and approved before gaining access to UK Biobank data".
7. **Each invited collaborator registers** in the same way.
8. **Submit.**

## Stage 3. Review

- **Registration:** UK Biobank aims to review each one within 10 working days.
- **Application:** sent to UK Biobank's epidemiologists within 10 working days of submission. Questions come through
  AMS. Reply quickly: UK Biobank says careful and prompt replies avoid delays.
- **Further review, if needed:** the Access Committee, which meets quarterly and may seek ethics advice.
- **If declined:** a written request for reconsideration within 3 months. It goes to the Committee's next quarterly
  meeting. If it is declined again, the same proposal cannot be resubmitted for 12 months.

## Stage 4. Approval, payment and MTA

- UK Biobank raises the fee request and sends the MTA by DocuSign to the PI and the signatory. Each collaborator
  institution signs its own MTA.
- **Approval lasts 90 days.** In that time EVA must pay and sign, or apply again.
- **Payment:** in pounds sterling, in one transaction, by Eva Health or the PI. Online in AMS, or by bank transfer
  against an invoice from AMS. Allow up to 10 working days for it to clear. UK Biobank does not fill in supplier forms.

## Stage 5. Training and data

- **Four modules before any access:** the MRC course (pass mark 70%), "Introduction to using UK Biobank", "Introduction
  to the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP)" and "Code repository training" (80% each).
- **Platform account and wallet:** £40 of starting credit, valid for 90 days after the first project is dispensed.
  Wallets start with a £250 spending limit, which can be raised. Payment by card, or by purchase order for £10,000 or
  more.
- **Data:** usually in the project within 24 hours once training is done and access is enabled.
- **Then:** run the registered plan, on the platform only.

## Stage 6. During and after the project

- **Annual report** every year. A late report suspends the project's access.
- **Results out of the platform:** only through UK Biobank's output checks, once they exist for EVA's project.
- **Before any publication or press release:** send it to UK Biobank at least 2 weeks before release. Warn UK Biobank
  in advance if it may draw significant public attention. Share press releases that mention UK Biobank with its press
  team first.
- **In every paper:** "UK Biobank" in the title or abstract, and the line "This research has been conducted using the
  UK Biobank Resource under application number [ ]."
- **Publish** within 6 months of the project end date, and a commensurate level of findings within the first 3 years.
- **Return the derived data** at least 1 month before the platform project expires (`APPLICATION.md`, section 7).
- **Extensions** of 12, 24 or 36 months can be requested before the project expires; "The request must be submitted
  within one month of the project end date." They are charged. Prices were not found.
- **At the end,** destroy the data and confirm it in writing to access@ukbiobank.ac.uk.
- **UK Biobank's name:** approved researchers may use it in communications about public-interest health research.
  "Any request to use the name of UK Biobank in a way that falls outside of these guidelines should be made in writing
  to the UK Biobank communications team." Ask before any marketing use.

## Timeline

No date can be promised while applications are closed. In normal operation UK Biobank gives these times:

| Registration review | Aim: 10 working days |

Measures of "biological age" built from routine blood tests have emerged as a low-cost way to judge how a body is ageing. A recent review of 81 such measures found that more than a third had been built with no validation at all, and most used one country's data. People and doctors cannot tell how far to trust them.

Eva Health is a preventive-health company in Spain. We built a biological age from six routine blood tests: albumin, alkaline phosphatase, C-reactive protein, creatinine, urea and gamma-glutamyl transferase. It uses a published method that links blood results to the risk of death, applied to US national health survey data. We wrote down our tests and pass marks before we built it. In US data held back for testing, it predicted death better than age and sex alone. It has not been published or tested outside the United States.

Our aims are:
1. To test the measure, unchanged, in UK Biobank. Does an older biological age mean a higher risk of death, beyond age and sex? Does it give men and women of each age about the right result? Does it work equally well across groups, such as ethnic background and area deprivation?
2. To find out whether other routine blood tests add useful information. Cystatin C, a blood test of kidney function, comes first. Any test that adds information may be added to our measure for clients, and its formula will be returned to UK Biobank.
3. To see how much a person's result changes between the first visit and the repeat visit, and how much it depends on how the samples were handled and tested.

We will publish our analysis plan before we see any data, and the results whether or not they support our measure. {"report": "**Recommendation: ship option 1 now.** It puts creatinine back into the lab-page biological age whenever a lab includes cystatin C, a blood marker of kidney filtration. The dashboard figure stays the same whenever the lab also has creatinine and a cystatin C inside EVA's plausibility bounds. In the same review, ask the physician whether they accept how the dashboard reads cystatin C. If not, follow with option 2.

Either way, plan the eGFR step. A laboratory's eGFR is the kidney filtration rate that many laboratories estimate and print on their reports. The eGFR step stops the dashboard counting creatinine twice through it. The step first needs a revalidation run, which repeats EVA's test of how well the figure predicts death.

If the physician will not countersign option 1, withhold the lab-page figure for labs with cystatin C instead. Option 3 is not recommended.

EVA shows two biological ages from one model, KDM v2.2. The lab-page figure is the Reference version. It is stored with each lab result, shown on the lab page, sent in the results email and read by the AI chat.

The dashboard figure is the Comprehensive version. It uses more markers. It averages the client's labs from the last 6 months. If there are fewer than two, it uses the last 12 months, or else the latest lab alone. That set of labs is the dashboard's window.

When a lab has a cystatin C result, the code deletes creatinine before either figure is calculated. The dashboard then uses cystatin C instead. The lab-page figure uses only the model's 14 core markers, and cystatin C is not one of them. So the lab-page figure ends up with no creatinine and nothing in its place.

It also skips the creatine adjustment. That is the amount EVA subtracts from creatinine for clients who take creatine. The minimum-marker check still counts cystatin C. So a lab-page figure can be published with one marker fewer than the stated minimum.

Only clients who upload a cystatin C result from another laboratory are affected. EVA's own laboratory does not send cystatin C. On upload, it enters only when someone picks it by hand. The group is probably small. Nobody has counted it, because no database was queried.

The lab-page part of the fix is the same in all three options. Option 1 ships it alone. The dashboard does not move for clients who also have creatinine and a plausible cystatin C. That is the narrowest change to put before a physician.

This matters because of EVA's model-selection decision. In it, the clinical and regulatory reviewer judged that a physician would not countersign KDM v2.2 at all. Option 1 also fits that decision: keep KDM v2.2 as a labelled estimate until version 3, and fix its claims now. Option 2 can follow later without touching the lab page again.

Going step by step has a cost. Each later step is another approval round and another visible move for these clients. Keeping only today's public disclosure is acceptable only for the days or weeks the approvals take.

All figures come from seven synthetic test personas run on the live code, not from client data. Base Panel means the tests in EVA's standard kit.

The test grid has 336 cases. Each persona is tested on the Base Panel and on a full panel. Each is tested with no cystatin C and at five cystatin C levels. Each is tested with and without a laboratory eGFR, and with and without creatine. 280 of the cases have cystatin C. Ages and changes are in years.

The method tag is the label stored with each lab-page figure that names the rule behind it.

No option fully matches version 3. Version 3 ignores results from other laboratories, and cystatin C only ever arrives from one. It also has no creatine adjustment. So creatine users who upload cystatin C will see their lab-page figure drop now. It will change again when version 3 launches, whichever option is chosen.

## The three options, ranked

Option 1 ranks first because it changes the least: no dashboard figure moves in the 336 grid cases. Option 2 ranks above option 3. Option 2 removes EVA's weakest kidney reading instead of adding it next to creatinine.

Option 3 moves the dashboard less than option 2. But it adds one more correlated kidney marker to a model that treats every marker as separate evidence. All three options keep BUN. Options 1 and 3, and step 1 of option 2, also keep a laboratory eGFR on top of creatinine or cystatin C.

All three options change the lab-page figure in the same way:
- It always uses creatinine and never cystatin C.
- The creatine adjustment reaches labs with cystatin C for the first time. It never did before. The deletion and the adjustment arrived in the same commit, and the deletion runs first.
- The minimum-marker check requires albumin and creatinine. It counts only markers the figure uses. This is the check of EVA's mortality validation run. That run tested how well the figure predicts death in NHANES, the US health survey the model was built on.

That shared change carries risks of its own:

| Shared risk | Test result | Suggested handling |
|---|---|---|
| Another laboratory's creatinine returns to the lab-page figure. One common method, uncompensated Jaffe, can read creatinine 30% or more high at low-normal values. Version 3 keeps other laboratories' results out of its age for this reason. It estimates this alone could move its age by up to 3.8 years | A creatinine 30% high would add 2.84 to 3.81 years to the lab page across the seven personas. This is an upper estimate | Uploads without cystatin C already carry this risk today. The broader fix is a separate decision, listed under other routes |
| A creatinine value in µmol/L entered without its unit is read as mg/dL. The deletion used to hide this for labs with cystatin C | Man 45, creatinine 88, cystatin C 0.85: lab page 52.34 today and 898.54 under every option. Dashboard 47.90 under option 1, 400.94 under option 2 and 392.91 under option 3 | Add a creatinine plausibility check, listed under related issues |
| The creatine adjustment can push creatinine down to zero | Woman 70, creatinine 0.35, creatine 20 g/day, cystatin C 1.0: lab page 85.59 today and 73.29 under every option | The physician signs off the adjustment's size |
| Labs with cystatin C but no creatinine lose their lab-page figure | Man 45: 52.34 today, none after | Count these labs before the change |
| Creatine users who upload cystatin C will see a second change at version 3 | See the note under the main table | Say so in the client notice |

**Option 1, recommended: fix the lab-page figure only.**

What it changes:
- The lab page changes as described above.
- The dashboard keeps today's rule: a cystatin C result replaces creatinine.
- The dashboard now ignores a cystatin C value outside EVA's own plausibility bounds of 0.2 to 8.0 mg/L. That catches most values typed in the wrong unit.

Who is affected:
- Every lab with a cystatin C result. Its lab-page figure changes when the lab is processed or reprocessed after the change. It becomes what the same lab gives without cystatin C.
- Creatine users' lab-page figures drop the most. The creatine adjustment now applies to them for the first time. That is why the physician must sign it.
- Real clients can move further than the personas. The size depends on their creatinine. Some clients have creatinine raised by muscle and uploaded cystatin C to show that. They will see a higher lab-page figure.
- Each affected client's dashboard is rebuilt at their next upload, value edit or reprocessing. It comes out the same for clients who also have creatinine and a plausible cystatin C. Two rare cases change. A cystatin C typed in the wrong unit is ignored. A window with cystatin C but no creatinine gets no dashboard figure. The dashboard then shows the latest lab's stored lab-page figure. That may be an old-rule value, or nothing if that lab was recalculated too.

Pros:
- Fixes every confirmed part of the defect. Creatinine is back. The creatine adjustment now reaches labs with cystatin C. The minimum-marker check counts only markers in use.
- It is the smallest change clients will see. No dashboard figure moves in the 336 grid cases.
- Removes the absurd dashboard result from a cystatin C typed in the wrong unit.
- Uses the kidney pair of standard blood-chemistry ages: creatinine and BUN. KDIGO 2024, the international kidney guideline, also makes the creatinine-based estimate the initial kidney test.
- Option 2 or the eGFR step can follow without touching the lab page again.

Cons:
- The dashboard still reads cystatin C with EVA's weakest model settings. A value at EVA's own optimal ceiling reads as a much older age.
- The dashboard's swap of creatinine for cystatin C was never validated.
- One cystatin C upload removes creatinine and the creatine adjustment from the client's whole dashboard average. Option 1 keeps that. So a creatine user's dashboard still rises by up to 2.11 years when cystatin C 0.85 enters the window. Their lab-page figure now falls.
- A laboratory eGFR still counts creatinine twice on the dashboard.
- The two figures read kidney function from different markers.
- The plausibility check catches wrong units and decimal slips that land outside 0.2 to 8.0 mg/L. It misses slips that stay inside those bounds, as the table shows. It has hard edges at its bounds. It checks averaged values, so a window that mixes units can pass.

A simpler variant changes only the lab-page code and leaves today's dashboard code in place. Give it the same plausibility check, and it matches option 1 in all 336 grid cases. The simpler variant has a cost. The dashboard would keep publishing figures without creatinine, which the validated minimum-marker check does not allow. The two figures would also follow different checks. The physician can choose either.

## Stored results and wording

Nothing is recalculated when the change ships. Labs stored before the fix keep their old lab-page figure. Results emails already sent cannot change. Some old labs and dashboards will still change without a separate decision:

| What happens | What it rewrites | Code |
|---|---|---|
| A value of a lab is edited | That lab, under the new rule | `src/app/api/biomarker-values/[id]/route.ts:203-205`; `src/lib/ai/regenerate-master.ts:102` |
| The summary of a client's latest lab is regenerated | That lab, when it has no master summary | `src/lib/ai/regenerate-master.ts:62` |
| The admin recalculation route runs | Every lab it covers. It must not run without approval | `src/app/api/admin/recalc-metrics/route.ts:56` |
| A client uploads, edits a value or has a lab reprocessed | The client's dashboard figure, from all labs in the window | `process-results.ts:616, :775`; `rolling-average-ba.ts:308-326` |

Every lab recalculation uses today's age in whole years and the client's current supplement list, not those at the draw. It also rewrites the lab's longevity score and grade, its version 3 shadow record and the client's dashboard figure. So a recalculated old lab can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the fix.

New labs get a new method tag, so lab-page figures under the old and new rules can be told apart. Today every stored figure carries the same tag. The tag name in the draft is a placeholder. The dashboard figure records only which version produced it, not which rule.

Suggested decision. First, ask someone with database access for a read-only count of labs with cystatin C, and of those without creatinine. Then choose how to treat old labs with cystatin C:

| Choice | Effect |
|---|---|
| Leave them, and add a dated line to the methodology page | No side effects. A client's history mixes two rules |
| Recalculate them with today's admin route after staging | One rule. But those labs also get today's age and supplements, and their scores and dashboards move. The CEO must accept these side effects explicitly |
| Build a recalculation that uses the age at the draw date and the supplements recorded with that lab, then run it after staging | One rule without those side effects. It needs building and its own approval. Not every lab has supplements on record |

The first choice is enough if the count is small. Otherwise prefer the third. The same approval should cover the automatic rewrites above.

{"report": "Today's model does not give an average person their own age back. Version 3 comes much closer, but in our Spanish-level test it reads slightly young.

Three things make today's model, KDM, read wrong. EVA's Spanish adjustment pushes everyone with the standard kit older. A vitamin D unit error pushes clients with vitamin D younger. The straight lines fitted on US data miss by age, even for Americans with American values. So the US fit is part of the cause. EVA's own "typical" personas are not typical either: their urea is above the US median.

How to centre version 3 for Spain is your decision. Your target is that an average Spaniard reads their own age. EVA's recorded plan sets the level from Spanish deaths instead. The two rules can point in opposite directions.

On creatine, keep creatinine as the base in both models. Start a pre-test instruction and a warning now. The warning must quote different numbers for each figure. Then replace today's dose formula with one flat correction. Bring in cystatin C later, as a calibrated option for declared users who do not pause. We found only two precedents for basing the kidney part of an age on cystatin C: one published UK Biobank panel and one consumer service.

Today's model will stay for about a year, and a physician may refuse to sign any change to it. I recommend withholding the lab-page figure until version 3, because it has the largest errors. Keep the dashboard figure as a labelled estimate.

No model or service checked adjusts a biological age for creatine. Every published blood-chemistry age checked uses creatinine, except Chan's reduced UK Biobank panel, which uses cystatin C instead. SiPhox reads its kidney age from creatinine- and cystatin-related markers, depending on the panel. These two are the only precedents found for the cystatin C route you asked about. The guidelines rely on two tools: test preparation and, where creatinine is in doubt, cystatin C.

Decisions you should know about:

- **Issue ids.** The id schema does not allow `|`, so an issue id is the four parts family, check, row key and side, joined with `--`, with each part made file-safe (`|` becomes `.`, `+` becomes `plus`, spaces become `_`). Because the id starts with the family, the refutation files `refutations/round-<n>/<id>-a.json` fall inside each family's owned paths. The script cannot import code, so it keeps its own copy of the id function, and a test fails if the two copies drift apart.
- **Judge file names.** The shard name is `<batch>.<family>.<family>...`. The judge file `judges/round-<n>/<lens>-<shard>.json` still starts with `<lens>-<batch>`, and also matches each family's owned pattern `judges/*/*<family>*.json`. A plain `<lens>-<batch>.json` would have failed the ownership check.
- **Check failures count for a family** when the failure key names one of the family's biomarker keys. Cross-marker failures (check K1) and app-level failures are left to the coherence and module units.
- **Failing checks go to the fixer without refuters.** They are recorded in the ledger as open script issues and closed by the script when the check clears. Refuters only test issues raised by judges.
- **Closing a confirmed issue.** After a fix round, the lens that raised it closes it by not raising it again.
- **Pass.** A family passes when no failure is attributed to it and no confirmed blocking issue remains. Blocked checks are never counted as passes. If any part was unreviewed, the family ends as `incomplete`, never `pass`.
- **Stop rules** apply per family in this order: pass, round limit, no net progress (new issues count), agent cap.
- **Agents that return nothing** are retried once at half scope, then recorded as unreviewed, which becomes a physician question when the family stops.
- **No-progress counts** come from the per-family counts that `ledger.js apply` prints. If that runner fails, the script falls back to its own count, and the unrecorded ledger items carry over to the next ledger run.
- **Ownership check.** Several families run at once in one working tree, so the runner checks the whole batch's `git status` (owned paths plus the loop's own outputs). It also checks and records each family's own files in `checks/<batch>-r<n>-changes.json`.
- **Parallel batches.** Each batch writes `checks/<batch>-run.json` and `scorecard-<batch>.md` rather than one shared `scorecard.md`, so parallel batches do not overwrite each other.
